The closest direct comparison is [Ask the GRU (2016)](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.02116): mean word-embedding encoder (Embed) versus stacked, order-sensitive GRU, each with/without auxiliary tag prediction. Cold-start Recall@50 on CiteULike-a/t: Embed 38.53/35.85, GRU 46.16/47.59; Embed-MTL 41.71/38.16, GRU-MTL 49.76/51.22. Crucial limitation: both encoders initialize embeddings with CBOW pretrained on 440,756 ACM abstracts; these results do not establish superiority under scratch-only training. Also, the GRU itself averages contextual hidden states—mean pooling after contextualization preserves order information that averaging raw token embeddings loses. Negation motivates the architecture through a same-unigram example, but is not evaluated with a controlled negation benchmark; product specifications and lexical shortcuts receive no targeted ablations.

I found no study establishing the complete requested comparison: scratch-trained pooling versus order-sensitive text encoding, with matched recommendation training and separate negation, specification-binding, sparse-item and shortcut tests. [SWEM (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09843) supplies adjacent pooling-versus-RNN/CNN evidence in text classification/matching, rather than recommendation-specific validation. The prior-art boundary therefore concerns demonstrated semantic preservation under these constraints, not introducing end-to-end text encoders or mean pooling. A useful proposed experiment would hold the GRU4Rec backbone and training protocol fixed, compare scratch token means against a small contextual text encoder, and report validation results by item frequency plus controlled word-order, negation-scope and numeric attribute-binding perturbations. Raw token means necessarily collapse identical token multisets; aggregate ranking gains alone cannot establish that the model learned those distinctions or avoided lexical shortcuts.
